cards.prompt: A café's review sorter learned that **"cold"** means unhappy, because it only ever saw it in reviews like "Cold food, slow service". Now it calls **"Lovely cold drinks on a hot day"** unhappy. What's the **best** fix?

options.text: Add happy reviews that use "cold", like "Ice-cold lemonade, really lovely"
Add more unhappy reviews that use "cold", like "Cold chips, cold tea"
Delete every training review with "cold" in it, happy or not
Add 100 copies of "Cold food, slow service", labelled unhappy

cards.explanation: The sorter never saw "cold" used happily, so **add examples where it is**. More unhappy "cold" reviews, or copies of one, only make it surer that cold means unhappy. Deleting them might fix this one review, but then it can't spot real complaints about cold food.

cards.prompt: A team labels 5,000 photos of cats and dogs in a big rush, and never checks them. About **1 in 10 dogs** ends up labelled "cat" by mistake. What will this most likely do to the model they train?

options.text: It learns some wrong lessons, so it mixes up more dogs
Nothing much: 9 in 10 labels are right, so it all evens out
It notices the wrong labels by itself and skips over them
It just takes longer to train, then ends up just as good

cards.explanation: A model learns from its labels exactly as they are. It can't tell a wrong label from a right one, so every dog labelled "cat" teaches it a **wrong lesson**, and it will mix up more dogs. That's why good training data has labels **checked**, not rushed.

cards.prompt: A plant model is tested on **10** new photos. It gets **4 wrong**. What is its accuracy?
cards.explanation: It got 6 of the 10 right, and each photo is worth 10%: **60%**. Accuracy counts the ones it got **right**.

cards.prompt: A bird-spotting app's makers say it scored **100%**. They tested it on the same photos it trained on. Is that a good test?

options.text: No: it may just have remembered those photos
Yes: 100% means it will never get a bird wrong
Yes, as long as the photos showed lots of different birds
No: a good test should use only the hardest bird photos

cards.explanation: Photos it trained on only test its **memory**: it may have **memorised them instead of learning** what birds look like. A fair test uses photos it has **never seen**, easy and hard, like the ones people will really take. Variety helps, but not if the model has seen them all before.

cards.prompt: Is each one a **fair** test of a model, or an **unfair** one?

items.label: Photos it never saw while training
Hard examples as well as easy ones
Photos in all kinds of light
Only the photos it already gets right

cards.explanation: A fair test uses **unseen**, **realistic** examples with a **mix** of difficulty. Picking photos it already gets right, or swapping photos until the score looks good, makes it look better than it is.

cards.prompt: A face-matching app works well for adults but often fails on children. What is the **best** fix?

options.text: Add many photos of children, then test on children
Add many more photos of adults, then test again
Make the app accept faces more easily

cards.explanation: The app is **biased** because children were missing from its training data. Add them, then **test on children** to check it worked. More adults add nothing about children; accepting faces more easily lets in the wrong people too; an overall score just hides the problem.

cards.prompt: A game's chat filter keeps blocking messages written in one language that lots of players use.

steps.text: Players who write in that language are getting blocked for normal messages. What should the game do?

choices.text: Ask those players to only write in English
choices.consequence: That blames the players. The problem is what the filter learned from.

choices.text: Add normal messages in that language to its training data, and test again
choices.consequence: Right: fill the gap in the data, then check it really works for those players.

choices.text: Make the filter block fewer messages for everyone
choices.consequence: That lets more mean messages through for everyone, and the filter still doesn't understand that language.

cards.explanation: The filter is biased because that language was missing from its training data. **Add the missing examples and test again**; never blame the people it gets wrong.

cards.prompt: Match each situation to the idea it shows.

pairs.left: Photos hidden from the model while it learns
It got 9 of 10 new photos right: 90%
Perfect on its training photos, poor on new ones
Understands one accent well, others badly

cards.explanation: **Test examples** are hidden while it learns; **accuracy** is the share it gets right; perfect on training but poor on new ones means it **memorised**; and working worse for some people is **bias**.
